nodes.label: Tashman (2000), Out-of-sample tests of forecasting accuracy
nodes.rationale: READ (14 pp), journal PDF on disk. THE canonical citation for rolling-origin evaluation. Section 3.1 names the three defects of a fixed origin; 4.3 the calendar argument; 4.4 states this study's rolling-window rationale verbatim in 2000 ('the comparison would be confounded if the second fit period were longer than the first'); 4.2 raises the recalibration objection; 6.2.1 grounds RelMSE by telling forecasters to avoid scale-dependent measures and use a ratio against a naive method. He does NOT establish that rolling-origin errors are statistically dependent — citing him for that would be citing what he did not write.

nodes.label: Bergmeir & Benitez (2012), On the use of cross-validation for time series predictor evaluation
nodes.rationale: Rolling-origin captures performance across differing conditions.

nodes.label: Hyndman & Athanasopoulos (2021), Forecasting: Principles and Practice
nodes.rationale: Section 5.10 — the textbook statement of time series cross-validation on rolling origins.

nodes.label: Giacomini & White (2006), Tests of conditional predictive ability
nodes.rationale: The econometric ground for a FIXED rolling window: their framework treats a forecast as the output of a method estimated on a finite, non-growing window, so estimation error does not vanish; an expanding window sits outside it.

nodes.label: Pesaran & Timmermann (2007), Selection of estimation window in the presence of breaks
nodes.rationale: Under structural breaks the optimal window is finite.

nodes.label: Rossi (2013), Advances in forecasting under instability
nodes.rationale: Out-of-sample performance is itself time-varying.

nodes.label: Bergmeir, Hyndman & Koo (2018), A note on the validity of cross-validation for evaluating autoregressive time series prediction
nodes.rationale: READ (18 pp), Monash working-paper copy (the July 2017 preprint, not the CSDA version of record). Cited AGAINST this study, which is the stronger move: Theorem 1 PROVES K-fold CV valid under A1 stationary/ergodic AR(p) in the target's own lags and correctly specified, A2 LOO consistency, A3 errors an MDS. A1 fails twice here (8-12 distinct variates, and stationarity is what RQ2/RQ3 exist to test) and A3 fails by construction at H = 24, where an optimal h-step error is MA(23) — the same fact section 9.2's rectangular truncation lag 23 already asserts. Their own remedy, a Ljung-Box test on pooled OOS residuals, is NOT currently run.

nodes.label: Cerqueira, Torgo & Mozetic (2020), Evaluating time series forecasting models
nodes.rationale: READ (28 pp), arXiv v1 on disk. The empirical half, on half-hourly/hourly/daily data: 11 estimators over 62 real series. On the 31 non-stationary series plain CV falls to among the worst; and the direction of bias is systematic — CV UNDER-estimates the loss while out-of-sample and prequential methods OVER-estimate it. That finding is the one for the manuscript: this study's headline is a null, and an optimistically biased estimator is precisely the one that manufactures skill that is not there.

nodes.label: Lopez de Prado (2018), Advances in Financial Machine Learning
nodes.rationale: Chapter 7 — the source of purging in a financial-ML setting, of the embargo and of CPCV itself.

nodes.label: Kaufman, Rosset & Perlich (2012), Leakage in data mining
nodes.rationale: The general taxonomy: leakage in FEATURES versus leakage in TRAINING EXAMPLES. The purge closes the second class; section 5.3's no-rolling-feature property closes the first, and this vocabulary is what makes 'structurally absent' checkable rather than asserted.

nodes.label: Hansen & Timmermann (2015), Equivalence between out-of-sample forecast comparisons and Wald statistics
nodes.rationale: The sample-split ratio is not innocuous: the power of an out-of-sample comparison depends on where the split falls, so a split chosen after seeing results is a researcher degree of freedom.

nodes.label: Gama et al. (2014), A survey on concept drift adaptation
nodes.rationale: Source of the blind (periodic) versus informed (drift-triggered) retraining distinction that RQ3 maps onto directly, and the nearest published relative of the falsification arm.

nodes.label: Lu et al. (2019), Learning under concept drift: a review
nodes.rationale: The recent review beside gama2014survey.

nodes.label: Zliobaite et al. (2015), Evaluation methods and decision theory for classification of streaming data with temporal dependence
nodes.rationale: Evaluation under temporal dependence is misleading without a persistence-style baseline — which is why section 7 makes Naive-RW mandatory.

nodes.label: Arian, Norouzi Mobarekeh & Seco (2024), Backtest overfitting in the machine learning era
nodes.rationale: READ (27 pp), Knowledge-Based Systems 305. Concludes CPCV BEATS walk-forward, and is answered from its own methods section: its walk-forward is CrossValidatorController('walkforward', n_splits=4) — a single backtest path its own 2.4.7 says 'tests the strategy only once', i.e. Tashman's fixed-origin design deprecated in 2000; its purgedkfold and combinatorialpurged each receive embargo=0.02 while walkforward receives NO purge at all, so the gap confounds combinatorial with purged; and its 2.4.2 endorses walk-forward for MODEL DECAY specifically, 'alongside other methods like CPCV'. Effect sizes: eta^2 = 0.0102 on PBO, 0.4523 vs 0.4005, walk-forward vs K-Fold p = 1.0.

nodes.label: Inoue, Jin & Rossi (2017), Rolling window selection for out-of-sample forecasting with time-varying parameters
nodes.rationale: Window length is a free parameter with real consequences and is estimable. THIS STUDY DOES NOT ESTIMATE IT — cite in Limitations, do not imply the 24 months were optimised.

nodes.label: Arnott, Harvey & Markowitz (2019), A backtesting protocol in the era of machine learning
nodes.rationale: The protocol-level authority for pre-registration, held-out test periods and reporting the full trial count.

nodes.label: Bailey & Lopez de Prado (2014), The deflated Sharpe ratio
nodes.rationale: The trial-count consequence of opening the test period once.

nodes.label: Makridakis, Spiliotis & Assimakopoulos (2018), Statistical and machine learning forecasting methods: concerns and ways forward
nodes.rationale: ML methods underperforming simple statistical benchmarks out of sample, under a rolling-origin protocol, over a large series collection. Read in the frame the protocol establishes, this study's 'no model beats Naive-RW' is a replication, not a bug.

nodes.label: Cameron, Gelbach & Miller (2008), Bootstrap-based improvements for inference with clustered errors
nodes.rationale: Supplies the clustered inference; the asymptotic refinement comes from bootstrapping the t-statistic, not beta-hat.

nodes.label: MacKinnon, Nielsen & Webb (2023), Cluster-robust inference: a guide to empirical practice
nodes.rationale: The companion to cameron2008bootstrap for the wild cluster bootstrap; restricted (WCR) rather than unrestricted, because WCU is severely size-distorted at small G.

nodes.label: Baur, Cahill, Godfrey & Liu (2019), Bitcoin time-of-day, day-of-week and month-of-year effects
nodes.rationale: Supplies the PREMISE for the 5-month spacing, which would otherwise read as numerology: month-of-year, day-of-week and time-of-day effects measured in Bitcoin specifically. The confound is documented in this asset; the spacing is the response to it.

nodes.label: Ma & Tanizaki (2019), The day-of-the-week effect on Bitcoin return and volatility
nodes.rationale: Measures the same calendar-effect class independently of baur2019calendar.

nodes.label: Figure 1 — the walk-forward scheme, two panels
nodes.rationale: report._figure1 draws from config.ORIGINS and nothing else. Upper panel: fifteen rows, one per origin, each carrying a 21-month training sub-block, a 3-month validation sub-block and six 30-day test blocks, with purge markers at both boundaries; the shape itself states that the window is rolling and fixed-length, that origins are 5 months apart, and that consecutive rows overlap by 79.2% of their training data. Lower panel: origin 1 resolved in days, because at the eight-year scale H = 24 h is 0.03% of the training window and thinner than the line drawn for it — the purge bands are drawn WIDER than 24 hours and the title says so.

nodes.label: Element 1 — multiple origins, not one train/test split
nodes.rationale: A single split estimates accuracy at one point in one regime; its error is an estimate with a sample size of one origin. Pack (1990), via Tashman, measured one method's MAPE at lead 4 moving 3.1% -> 5.8% across test periods.

nodes.label: Element 2 — chronological ordering preserved; no K-fold, no shuffling
nodes.rationale: RQ2's independent variable is time since training. Any scheme that reorders blocks leaves it undefined.

nodes.label: Element 3 — rolling 24-month window, not expanding
nodes.rationale: With an expanding window the training-set size grows with each origin, so model age cannot be separated from training data volume — and RQ2 is a claim about age. Tashman's section 4.4 states this study's exact argument, in 2000.

nodes.label: Element 4 — window length = 24 months
nodes.rationale: A sample-budget choice: 13,545-15,217 training windows on the feature frame against 12 x 96 input dimensions. The window length is a free parameter this study FIXES rather than estimates, and Limitations must say so.

nodes.label: Element 5 — 21/3 train-validation split inside the window
nodes.rationale: Early stopping and ridge alpha are selected somewhere, and that somewhere must be inside the training window and before the origin.

nodes.label: Element 6 — H-step purge at BOTH boundaries
nodes.rationale: A training window whose 24-step target reaches past the boundary carries post-boundary observations into training. At the train->validation boundary the contaminated split is the one governing MODEL SELECTION (D24).

nodes.label: Element 7 — no embargo, and why the channel is structurally absent
nodes.rationale: An embargo guards the REVERSE channel: a test-period bar influencing a training-set feature value. No feature here uses a rolling window (section 5.3), so that channel does not exist. The argument is CONDITIONAL on section 5.3 and must be re-derived if any rolling feature is ever added.

nodes.label: Element 8 — six 30-day test blocks, no retraining inside them
nodes.rationale: This is periodic (blind) retraining evaluated at a fixed cadence; RQ3 asks what the cadence should be, which requires observing performance as a function of block index.

nodes.label: Element 9 — out-of-sample is everything right of the origin
nodes.rationale: There is no fourth split. A forecaster at o has seen everything before it and nothing after.

nodes.label: Element 10 — errors clustered by origin, not pooled as 90 independent cells
nodes.rationale: Consecutive origins share 79.2% of their training data (58.3 / 37.5 / 16.7% at strides 2-4), so A(i,b) series are dependent by construction. The dependence argument is THIS STUDY'S OWN, from D28's overlap arithmetic. What Tashman supplies instead is his section 6.3: Fildes et al. (1998) over 263 series found the relative RANKING of methods changed appreciably as the origin varied.

nodes.label: Element 11 — CPCV considered and rejected
nodes.rationale: CPCV reorders blocks non-chronologically, leaving time-since-training undefined, and assumes DGP stability across blocks — the assumption this study tests. Cite the objecting paper and ANSWER it; ignoring it is the reviewable failure.

nodes.label: Element 12 — test period opened once, after the design is frozen
nodes.rationale: The Stage 5 gate that repositioned the title ran on VALIDATION, not on test (D27).

nodes.label: Element 13 — the result: no model beats Naive-RW
nodes.rationale: Read in the frame the protocol establishes, this is a replication, not a bug.

nodes.label: Unlicensed choice 1 — the 5-month origin spacing
nodes.rationale: NO published protocol prescribes it. With origins spaced s months and 30-day blocks the calendar month block b lands on is m0 + s*i + (b-1) mod 12, so the months visited form a coset of size 12/gcd(s,12). At s = 6 each block index visits only two calendar months, so a significant beta1 would be observationally equivalent to a month-of-year effect. Only s coprime to 12 decouples the two; among those, 5 maximises the origin count subject to the data span. Present it as a reasoned choice with a stated consequence, never as borrowed protocol.

nodes.label: Unlicensed choice 2 — the falsification arm (fresh model at o + 90 d)
nodes.rationale: Standard rolling-origin protocols do not carry one. It exists because aged-model decay and calendar difficulty are otherwise observationally equivalent: if the aged-minus-fresh gap is zero while beta1 < 0, then beta1 is calendar, not age. Report it on RelMSE, NEVER on scaler-space MSE (D60i) — the two arms carry different sigma_g.

nodes.label: Unlicensed choice 3 — the six-block, 180-day test span
nodes.rationale: A convention, not an optimum. Its consequence is stated rather than hidden: b* resolves only to 30-day granularity out to 180 days, so 'no decay detected within 180 days' is a RIGHT-CENSORED result and must be worded as one — not the situation that occurred (D60b).

nodes.label: The recalibration objection (Tashman section 4.2), answered in three parts
nodes.rationale: The sharpest objection a referee who has actually read Tashman will raise, and it was found by reading him rather than by citing him: 'Updating without recalibrating imposes an arbitrary handicap.' Three things separate the cases and all three belong in the manuscript. (1) His mechanism is a static regression where a new data point changes neither inputs nor coefficients; here the INPUTS move — each of the 720 forecasts per block is issued from a different 96-bar window, only the weights are fixed. (2) The frozen weights ARE the measurement: RQ3 asks what accuracy costs when a model is left in place. (3) Recalibration does happen, every five months at each of the fifteen origins, and the falsification arm is precisely the recalibrated comparator he asks for, run at one interior point. Saying only the third invites the reader to ask why the interior of the test span was left alone.

nodes.label: Why the strongest paper FOR cross-validation does not license it here
nodes.rationale: Section 2.1 exists because 'K-fold CV is fine for time series, Bergmeir proved it' is the single most likely challenge to section 8, and the answer is not a preference but an assumption check that either passes or fails. A1 fails twice (multivariate inputs; stationarity is the thing RQ2/RQ3 test) and A3 fails by construction at H = 24 (MA(23) errors cannot be an MDS) — using K-fold CV would contradict the rectangular variance estimator the same manuscript defends. Scope stated honestly: both papers study univariate, purely autoregressive, one-step-ahead forecasting; they are cited for the assumption boundary and the direction of the bias, not as evidence about this architecture.

nodes.label: Answering arian2024backtest from its own methods section
nodes.rationale: Section 4.2. Three facts about their code, stated FIRST: single path (n_splits=4, their own 2.4.7 calls it 'a single backtest path ... it tests the strategy only once'), unpurged (walkforward receives neither times= nor embargo=0.02 while the CV variants do, so the measured gap confounds combinatorial with purged), and their 2.4.2 endorses walk-forward for MODEL DECAY specifically. The estimand argument — PBO and DSR measure strategy-SELECTION overfitting among candidates competing on one return series — is stated LAST, because leading with it reads as special pleading while the two facts about their code do not. This is Related Work material, not only a defensive paragraph.

nodes.label: What Tashman also settles about the metrics (section 6.2.1)
nodes.rationale: Avoid scale-dependent error measures such as RMSE and MAD when averaging over series that differ in scale or volatility; use a RATIO against a naive method instead, which 'standardizes the component series for degree of change and, hence, degree of forecasting difficulty'. RelMSE = MSE_model / MSE_naive is the squared-error analogue, and that phrase is D05's argument written in 2000. D60i — no cross-origin comparison on scaler-space MSE, because each origin carries its own sigma_g — is the same rule reached the hard way, by a units artefact that made a falsification-arm number read backwards.

nodes.label: Status of the citations — resolved is not read
nodes.rationale: Every DOI was confirmed against Crossref by DOI LOOKUP, not by relevance search (D89 explains why the distinction matters). verified=doi-resolved means the identifier and metadata are right and the source has NOT been read end to end; section 13.3 forbids citing above the tier actually reached. Of 70 bib entries, 8 are read, 53 doi-resolved, 8 artifact, 2 screened, against a 35-45 reference budget — the largest single piece of work left in the project, and no part of it is computational. Reading the four load-bearing entries changed the DOCUMENT rather than only its flags: element 3 gained Tashman's 4.4 sentence, element 10 LOST a claim he does not make, and sections 4.1 and 4.2 exist only because the sources were opened.

nodes.label: Draft paragraph for manuscript section 3.6
nodes.rationale: Section 5 is a ready draft of the walk-forward methodology paragraph with every bibtex key in place, so the manuscript prose and this document's element table cannot drift apart.
